answer.rationale: p99 latency is climbing on the write path while settlement writes are at peak. The release carries a compliance-mandated security patch and must not be reverted, so rollback_release is ruled out. The write-path latency symptom points at capacity saturation, not a dependency failure, so circuit breakers don't match the signal. Regional failover is heavier than this needs and would burn the one-intervention budget on riskier movement; memory_b2 confirms failover is fast and reversible, but it is not the right tool for a steady write-path climb. Read-replica routing (memory_b5) relieves read load on the primary, but the current hot spot is the write path, not reads. memory_b3 is the load-bearing precedent here: provisioning headroom before a retail peak kept queue depth flat across the entire promotional window. That maps cleanly onto a small, guarded capacity bump on the write path now, while settlement is hot, to absorb the surge without losing writes or touching the release. Verifying memory_b3 to confirm the prior provisioning move was the specific lever (and not, say, a config change) before committing. Verifying memory_b6 as a secondary check, because the release just went out two hours ago and memory_b6 shows staged gating can catch a bad build fast if the latency climb turns out to be build-caused rather than capacity-caused; I want that read fresh before I commit so I am not surprised by a canary-flagged regression mid-intervention. If either verification changes the picture, the next window's action list reorders around it; I am not pre-committing beyond this one capacity move.
